planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this dwarf triandrus daffodil naturalizes well in rock gardens and front-of-border plantings.

directions: Plant bulbs 4 to 5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade in fall. Bred by Brent Heath and named for his mother, this Division 5 triandrus daffodil carries two or more nodding, slightly reflexed white flowers per stem, each centered with a cup that opens apricot-pink and fades to a softer blush as it ages. Its small, drooping blooms and modest stature make it a charming choice for rock gardens, raised beds, or the front of a mixed perennial border, where it is best viewed up close. Let foliage ripen and yellow naturally after bloom before cutting it back, and leave clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Tricollet is a split-corona (collar) daffodil whose propeller-like orange cup lies flat against a pure white perianth.

directions: Plant bulbs 5 to 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Registered in the Netherlands in 1969, Tricollet is a Division 11 collar daffodil whose six corona segments split for more than half their length and spread flat against the broad white perianth in a bright, propeller-shaped burst of orange. The dramatic two-tone contrast reads almost like a different flower form from a distance and makes it a standout in mixed daffodil plantings or cut arrangements. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize over the years.

common_name: Sabine Hay Daffodil (Small-Cupped Coral and Coppery-Orange Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Sabine Hay is a Division 3 small-cupped daffodil with coppery-orange petals and a coral-red cup, blooming mid-to-late spring.

directions: Plant bulbs 5 to 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Registered in England in 1970, this Division 3 small-cupped daffodil opens with rounded, rich coppery-orange petals surrounding a shallow, eye-catching coral-red cup, with the petal color softening toward creamy yellow as the mid-to-late-spring flowers age. The warm, saturated coloring stands out against the more common yellow and white daffodils and holds up well as a cut flower. Let the foliage yellow and die back naturally after bloom, and leave clumps undisturbed to build into drifts over successive seasons.
